title: "Confirming" means affirming what God revealed, not endorsing the texts in circulation

rows.thesis: The Quran confirms the revelation God gave to Moses and Jesus. It never confirms the later compilations as they stood in the 7th century, and Christians accept the same kind of selective confirmation when Jesus confirms the Torah.
rows.arg:
P1 The Quran tells believers to believe in what Allah revealed to Moses and Jesus (2:136; 3:3). 
 P2 The books Jews and Christians held in the 7th century were not entirely revelation: the Gospels, for example, are accounts written about Jesus by others, not the Injil revealed to him. 
 ∴ The Quran's confirmation covers the revealed content within those books, not the books as wholes. This is a general confirmation, not a blanket one, and the dilemma's first premise is false.
rows.ev:
The idiom. Musaddiqan lima bayna yadayhi means "confirming what came before it" (Lane's Lexicon : bayna yadayhi , "before it" in time). It describes the Quran's relationship to earlier revelation, not to particular manuscripts.

 Jesus' "confirmation". Jesus confirmed the Torah (Matt 5:17) and told people to obey the teachers on Moses' seat (Matt 23:2-3), yet he set aside the Torah's rules on oaths (Matt 5:33-37 against Num 30:2) and "eye for an eye" (Matt 5:38-39 against Exod 21:24). Christians don't say Jesus contradicted himself. Confirmation is not a blanket endorsement of every line.

 Fulfilment. "Believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you" (2:41). A key sense of confirmation is fulfilment: the Quran and the Prophet ﷺ are what the earlier scriptures foretold (7:157; 61:6), the same way Christians say Jesus "confirmed" the Old Testament by fulfilling it. It also confirms the shared creed: one God, prophets, angels, judgement.

 Naming the corrupted book. The Quran can call the book in their hands "the Torah" because that is what they claim it is, as Joseph calls the idols "lords" when addressing his fellow prisoners (12:39), and because it used to be that, as "give the orphans their property" (4:2) is said of orphans who have grown up.

 Nicolai Sinai , an Oxford scholar, explains that the Quran's term muhaymin (5:48) makes a stronger claim than "confirming": the Quran is the "ultimate arbiter" over Jewish and Christian scripture, and its confirmation involves "authoritative modification and rectification".

 
 Tap to enlarge Nicolai Sinai, Key Terms of the Qur'an , p. 707: muhaymin makes a stronger claim than musaddiq ; the Quran stands over earlier scripture

title: The Quran describes the earlier scriptures as altered, and every early Muslim authority agreed

rows.thesis: The Quran names at least five kinds of corruption, and from the Companions onward Muslim scholars understood that the books in Jewish and Christian hands had been changed.
rows.arg:
P1 If the Quran explicitly describes the People of the Book changing, concealing and writing scripture, it does not regard their texts as preserved. 
 P2 It describes concealment, twisting with the tongue, writing with their own hands, exchanging words and moving words from their places; Ibn Abbas, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Taymiyya and many others say the texts were altered. 
 ∴ The Quran and the early Muslims did not believe the Bible was preserved, so "the early Muslims believed the Bible was intact" is false.
rows.ev:
Five kinds of tahrif in the Quran. 

 
 Concealment: "you conceal the truth while you know it" (2:42; 3:71; 3:187).

 Twisting with the tongue: "a party of them twist their tongues with the Book so you think it is from the Book, but it is not" (3:78).

 Writing by hand: "woe to those who write the book with their own hands, then say, this is from Allah" (2:79).

 Exchanging words: "the wrongdoers changed the word to other than what was said to them" (2:59).

 Moving words from their places: "they distort words from their places" (4:46; 5:13).

 And making scripture into pages, "showing some and hiding much" (6:91).

 
 The Companions. Ibn Abbas: "How can you ask the People of the Book about anything when your Book… is the most recent? Allah has told you that the People of the Book changed and altered what Allah wrote, and wrote the book with their own hands and said 'this is from Allah'" (Bukhari 7363; 2685).

 The scholars. Ibn Kathir on 3:78: the books in their hands have certainly been changed, added to and subtracted from. Ibn Taymiyya held a middle view: some wording and much meaning were altered. Al-Jahiz noted that two of the four Evangelists were not disciples and that the Gospels' contradictions show they were not protected from error. Al-Qadi Isma'il ibn Ishaq explained the difference: Allah entrusted the Torah to its people to preserve (5:44, " bima ustuhfizu ", "what they were entrusted to preserve"), and they could fail, but He took the Quran's preservation on Himself (15:9). The list includes Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Ka'b, Muqatil, Tabari, Ibn Hazm, al-Juwayni, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi. A 7th-century Syriac dispute between the patriarch John of Sedra and an Arab emir (c. 644) already shows the Muslim side questioning the Gospels.

 The "tahrif of meaning only" quote. A statement in Bukhari's chapter headings says "no one can remove a word from Allah's books, but they misinterpret them". It is a mu'allaq comment traced to Wahb ibn Munabbih or Bukhari's own gloss, not a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ, and Ibn Abbas' explicit statement in the same book contradicts it.

title: "None can change the words of Allah" is about His decree, not the Bible's text

rows.thesis: Verses like 6:115 and 10:64 say no one can change Allah's kalimat , meaning His decrees and promises. The Quran guarantees preservation only for itself (15:9), while the Torah was entrusted to humans (5:44).
rows.arg:
P1 If "the words of Allah" in these verses meant every earlier scripture, the Quran would contradict its own statements that people altered those scriptures (2:79; 4:46). 
 P2 In context, kalimat Allah means His decree and promise: that He will help His messengers (6:34) and give glad tidings to believers (10:64). 
 ∴ These verses don't say the Bible can't be altered.
rows.ev:
6:34 : "Messengers before you were denied, and they were patient… until Our help came to them. None can alter the words of Allah." The "words" are His promise of help.

 10:64 : "For them are glad tidings in the life of this world and the Hereafter. No change is there in the words of Allah." The promise of glad tidings.

 18:27 : "Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord; none can change His words." This concerns the Quran, revealed to the Prophet ﷺ.

 Tabari and Qatada explain kalimat as His decrees and promises.

 15:9 promises the preservation of "the Reminder" (the Quran) by Allah Himself. 5:44 says the rabbis judged by "what they were entrusted to preserve of Allah's Book", making them the guardians, and humans can fail.

 The word "dhikr". 16:43 tells people to "ask the people of the Reminder ( ahl al-dhikr ) if you do not know". There dhikr refers to the earlier revelation and its people, who can be asked about shared basics (that earlier prophets were men). In 15:9, the commentators agree, dhikr is the Quran. The meaning depends on context.

 15:9 
 وَلَقَدْ كُذِّبَتْ رُسُلٌ مِّن قَبْلِكَ فَصَبَرُوا… حَتَّىٰ أَتَاهُمْ نَصْرُنَا ۚ وَلَا مُبَدِّلَ لِكَلِمَاتِ اللَّهِ

"If God could preserve the Quran, why not the Torah?"

title: 10:94: "Ask those who read the Book before you"

rows.thesis: 10:94 is a conditional, rhetorical statement directed through the Prophet ﷺ to doubters, about the stories of Noah and Moses just told; the people to ask are the believing People of the Book who recognised the Prophet. It does not endorse their scriptures as preserved.
rows.arg:
P1 A verse must be read in its context and with the rest of the Quran's statements about the People of the Book. 
 P2 10:94 follows the stories of Noah, Moses and Pharaoh (10:71-93); it is conditional ("if you are in doubt") and ends "so never be among the doubters"; the commentators say the Prophet neither doubted nor asked; the Quran elsewhere calls the People of the Book unreliable witnesses and praises those of them who believed. 
 ∴ 10:94 refers to confirmation of the prophetic stories by believing scholars like Abdullah ibn Salam, not to an endorsement of the Bible.
rows.ev:
Context. The preceding verses tell how Noah was rejected and saved, and how Moses and Aaron confronted Pharaoh, who drowned. These are in Genesis 6-9 and Exodus 2-14, and anyone who read the Torah could confirm them.

 Rhetorical. "If you are in doubt" does not mean the Prophet doubted. Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "He neither doubted nor asked" (Tabari). The grammarians Tha'lab and al-Mubarrad, and al-Qurtubi, explain that the address is to the doubting listener through the Prophet.

 Who to ask. Ibn Abbas and Tabari: those of the People of the Book who knew Muhammad ﷺ from their books and believed, such as Abdullah ibn Salam (46:10; 13:43; 28:52-53). Ibn Kathir links it to their recognising him "as they recognise their own sons" (2:146).

 The Prophet's own instruction. "Do not believe the People of the Book and do not deny them; say: we believe in Allah and what was revealed" (Bukhari 4485). That makes no sense if 10:94 told him to treat their books as authoritative.

 Ibn Taymiyya ( al-Jawab al-Sahih ) lists what the earlier books still testify to: the monotheism of the prophets, that messengers were human, how nations treated their prophets, the core of religion, and the signs of Muhammad ﷺ.

title: The Quran's Torah and Injil are revelations, not the Bible's books, and there was no Arabic Bible

rows.arg:
P1 The Quran's terms must be defined by the Quran's usage. 
 P2 The Quran says Moses was given the Tablets and the Torah, and Jesus was taught the Injil by God (3:48; 5:46). The New Testament Gospels are, by Christian admission, accounts written by others about Jesus. 
 P3 The earliest Arabic translations of the Bible date from the 8th-9th centuries. 
 ∴ The Quran's "Injil" is not the New Testament, and the Prophet ﷺ had no access to a written Arabic Bible.
rows.ev:

 No Arabic Bible. Bruce Metzger: the earliest Arabic Bible translations probably date from the 8th century. The oldest dated Arabic Gospel manuscript, Vatican Arabic 13, is from the 9th century. Sidney Griffith ( The Bible in Arabic ) agrees, and notes that the Gospel the Quran confirms is not the Gospel as Christians had it.

title: The Quran did not copy the apocrypha

rows.thesis: The Quran shares some stories with non-canonical texts (Jesus' clay birds, "what no eye has seen", Moses in Midian), but the parallels are with older, shared traditions, the Quran's versions differ in theologically significant ways, and the supposed sources are often later than the Quran.
rows.arg:
P1 Copying requires access to the source, and the copy should reproduce the source's distinctive features. 
 P2 The Quran's versions lack the distinctive features of the alleged sources (and sometimes correct them), the sources were not available in Arabic, and some are later than the Quran. 
 ∴ The parallels reflect shared earlier tradition, not copying.
rows.ev:
The clay birds (3:49; 5:110) and the Infancy Gospel of Thomas. In the Infancy Gospel, a five-year-old Jesus makes twelve sparrows on the Sabbath, quarrels about the Sabbath, and elsewhere kills a teacher and a child with curses and is worshipped. In the Quran, Jesus as a prophet makes "the form of a bird", and it becomes a bird "by Allah's permission" ( bi-idhni-llah ), repeated pointedly. The Quran takes nothing of the Infancy Gospel's distinctive content and adds what it lacks: dependence on God. The Infancy Gospel's oldest fragment is a 4th/5th-century papyrus, and complete manuscripts of the story are medieval. Scholars like Fred Lapham think some stories go back to early oral tradition, and Irenaeus (c. 180) knew one. John 21:25 itself says much of what Jesus did was never written. Even the critic Sean Anthony concedes the Quran did not copy the Infancy Gospel.

 "What no eye has seen" (hadith qudsi, Bukhari 3244; 1 Cor 2:9). Paul introduces it with "as it is written", so he is quoting an older source. The same saying appears, attributed to Jesus, in the Gospel of Thomas (17), in 1 Clement (34:8), the Gospel of Judas and other texts. Origen thought Paul was citing an apocryphon (Clivaz and Schulthess). A shared earlier prophetic saying is not copying from Paul.

 Moses in Midian (28:22-28) "confused with Jacob". The "Jacob" details critics cite (a rock on the well, seven years' service, a daughter named Leah) are in later commentaries and Isra'iliyyat, not the Quran (Gabriel Reynolds, The Qur'an in Its Context ). Meeting a wife at a well is a common ancient motif (Gen 24 with Rebekah), and working in place of a bride-price was a known custom (Kitchen). The proposed rabbinic source, Exodus Rabbah 1:32, dates to the 10th century or later. The Quran's eight to ten years are not Jacob's seven.

 Manichaeans. The Encyclopaedia of Islam describes Central Arabia as "hermetically sealed" against Byzantine and Persian missions, and François de Blois finds no evidence the Meccans knew the southern Babylonian sects.
rows.obj:
"Even if not copied directly, Muhammad heard these stories orally."
 Then the source was oral tradition circulating among Christians, which may preserve true events about Jesus that the canonical Gospels did not record (John 21:25). The Quran presents its account as revelation that corrects the theology around such stories.

 “The Quran copies a 2nd-century fairy tale about clay birds.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer The Quran's account shares only the miracle itself, and puts it "by Allah's permission", while dropping the Infancy Gospel's child Jesus who kills people. Irenaeus already knew stories from this tradition in 180, so it may preserve an early memory. A shared event isn't a copy.

title: "The Jews say Ezra is the son of God" (9:30)

rows.thesis: 9:30 reports what a group of Jews said, not the official creed of all Judaism. Jewish texts of the period exalted Ezra to a near-heavenly status, the Jews of Medina never denied the verse, and the Quran's style uses a general term for a particular group.
rows.arg:
P1 The Quran reports sayings "with their mouths", not formal creeds. 
 P2 Jewish literature around the time exalted Ezra as the restorer of the Torah who was taken up to live with God's "son"; the scribal figure (Ezra/Enoch) was elevated to angelic status; and the Jews of Medina, who were hostile to the Prophet, never objected that no Jew said this. 
 ∴ 9:30 accurately reports a belief held by some Jews, and is not an error.
rows.ev:
"With their mouths." The verse continues: "that is their saying with their mouths; they imitate the saying of those who disbelieved before" (9:30). It describes speech, not scripture.

 Ezra exalted. In 4 Ezra (late 1st century CE), Ezra restores the lost scriptures by divine inspiration and is told: "you shall be taken up from among men, and henceforth you shall live with My Son" (4 Ezra 14:9). Ezra 7:6 already describes him as a scribe on whom "the hand of the LORD his God" rested and who was granted all he asked. Jewish tradition fused the figure of the inspired Scribe (Ezra/Enoch) with angelic status; in 3 Enoch, Enoch becomes Metatron, called "the lesser YHWH" (3 Enoch 12:5). Angels were called "sons of God" in Jewish texts (Gen 6:2; Job 1:6).

 Scholars. Gordon Newby ( A History of the Jews of Arabia ) argues Ezra could be counted among the bene elohim in Arabian Jewish circles; Reuven Firestone finds it plausible that a Jewish group elevated Ezra to near-divine status.

 Medina's Jews didn't object. Ibn Abbas reports that Jewish leaders of Medina (Sallam ibn Mishkam and others) told the Prophet ﷺ they could not follow him because he did not hold Uzayr to be the son of Allah. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr says the saying came from Finhas ibn 'Azura. Ibn al-'Arabi notes that the Jews of Medina never objected to the verse, which they would have if it were baseless.

Al-Qurtubi explains that Arabic can use a general term for part of a group ( itlaq ism al-kull 'ala al-ba'd ), as in 3:173, "the people said to them, the people have gathered against you", where "the people" was a few men. The Bible does the same: "the world cannot receive him" (John 14:17).

title: Mary and the Trinity (5:116; 5:73)

rows.thesis: The Quran does not define the official Trinity as Father, Son and Mary. It condemns every form of "God is one of three", and it accurately condemns the deification of Mary that was real among Christians of its time.
rows.arg:
P1 The Quran addresses what Christians of its era actually believed and practised, not only the creeds of councils. 
 P2 5:73 rejects saying "Allah is the third of three"; 5:116 asks whether Jesus told people to take him and his mother as gods, which condemns the worship of Mary; and there is ample evidence of Mary being treated as divine. 
 ∴ The Quran's statements are accurate descriptions of real Christian belief and practice.
rows.ev:
What the verses say. 5:73: "They have disbelieved who say Allah is the third of three." 5:116: "Did you say to people, take me and my mother as gods besides Allah?"  Mary worshipped. Epiphanius describes the Collyridians, women who offered cakes to Mary as to a goddess ( Panarion 79). The Christian historian Eutychius (Sa'id ibn Batriq, 9th-10th century) mentions "Mariamites" who held Jesus and his mother to be two gods besides God.

 Mary as divine protector. (5:17); "they both used to eat food" (5:75).

 Later Marian devotion. Alphonsus Liguori's The Glories of Mary says "at the command of Mary all obey, even God". Popes still entrust the world and people's salvation to her. Calvin mocked churches displaying vials of Mary's milk.
rows.ar:

 5:116

 5:73
rows.obj:
"Taking Mary as a 'god' isn't Catholic doctrine; Catholics only venerate her."

title: "O sister of Aaron" (19:28)

rows.thesis: The Prophet ﷺ himself explained that the Israelites named people after earlier prophets and righteous figures; "sister" means kinswoman or descendant; and Luke places Mary's relative Elizabeth among "the daughters of Aaron".
rows.arg:
P1 If the Prophet ﷺ answered this objection directly and the usage is confirmed in Semitic languages and the Gospels, it is not an error. 
 P2 When Christians of Najran raised it, the Prophet ﷺ said they used to name people after the prophets and righteous before them (Muslim 2135); "sister" in Arabic and Hebrew means a female relative or tribeswoman; and Luke 1:5 and 1:36 make Mary a relative of a "daughter of Aaron". 
 ∴ "Sister of Aaron" calls Mary a kinswoman of Aaron's line, not Moses' sister.
rows.ev:
The Prophet's answer. Al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba was asked by the Christians of Najran how the Quran could call Mary "sister of Aaron" when Moses lived long before Jesus. The Prophet ﷺ said: "They used to name people after the prophets and righteous people before them" (Muslim 2135).

 "Sister" as kin. The Prophet ﷺ told his wife Safiyya, of Jewish descent, to answer taunts by saying "my father is Aaron, my uncle is Moses" (Tirmidhi 3894). The Quran calls Hud "brother" of 'Ad (7:65) and Salih "brother" of Thamud (7:73), meaning kinsman.

 Luke. Elizabeth "was of the daughters of Aaron" (Luke 1:5), and the angel calls Mary her "relative" (Luke 1:36). By the same Semitic usage, Mary could be called "sister of Aaron". Commentators like Ellicott and Poole draw this inference from Luke.

 No confusion in the Quran. The Quran never puts Moses or Aaron in the same scene as Jesus, and says many messengers came between them (2:87; 5:46). Gregory of Nyssa saw Miriam, "the sister of Aaron" (Exod 15:20), as a type of Mary; modern scholars like Michael Marx read 19:28 as deliberate typology, not confusion.

 The Bible repeats names. There are several Zechariahs and several Marys in the Bible; repeated names don't imply confusion.
rows.ar:
يَا أُخْتَ هَارُونَ مَا كَانَ أَبُوكِ امْرَأَ سَوْءٍ وَمَا كَانَتْ أُمُّكِ بَغِيًّا
 19:28
rows.obj:
"Mary's father is called 'Imran, Moses' father's name, so the Quran confuses the two Marys."
 Mary's father 'Imran (3:35) is a different person, and Christians themselves didn't know her father's name from the Gospels (later tradition says Joachim). Repeated family names, especially in priestly lines, were normal.
rows.rebut:

 “The Quran confuses Mary the mother of Jesus with Miriam the sister of Moses.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer The Prophet ﷺ himself answered this: Israelites named people after earlier prophets (Muslim 2135). Luke puts Mary among the relatives of the "daughters of Aaron". And the Quran says plainly that many messengers came between Moses and Jesus.

title: The names Yahya and 'Isa

rows.thesis: The Quran's "Yahya" is not a misspelling of Yuhanna; it says God gave John a name no one had borne before, which matches Luke. "'Isa" is the Arabised form of the Syriac name of Jesus, attested before Islam.
rows.arg:
P1 A name is an error only if it contradicts the evidence of the person's real name or the language's usage. 
 P2 The Quran says God gave John a name "We had not given to anyone before" (19:7), and Luke says his relatives protested that no one in the family had that name (Luke 1:59-61). The Quran's name Yahya is unknown before Islam, which fits the claim. 'Isa reflects Syriac Isho' and appears in a pre-Islamic Arabian inscription. 
 ∴ Neither name is an error.
rows.ev:
19:7. "O Zechariah, We give you good news of a boy whose name is Yahya; We have not made ( naj'al ) for anyone before him a namesake." Arthur Jeffery admits the name Yahya has no trace in earlier literature, which is what the verse claims: a unique name from God. Luke 1:59-61 records that the family objected: "none of your relatives is called by this name." Some commentators also read samiyy as "equal", as in 19:65 ("do you know any equal ( samiyy ) to Him?").

 'Isa. Syriac Christians called Jesus Isho' . Ahmad al-Jallad has identified the name in a pre-Islamic Safaitic (North Arabian) inscription, and Sidney Griffith calls the Syriac origin "the most reasonable explanation". Names change form between languages, like "Jesus" from Greek Iesous from Hebrew Yeshua .

 19:7
rows.obj:

title: The story of the cow (2:67-74)

rows.thesis: Critics say the Quran confused the red heifer (Numbers 19) with the heifer of an unsolved murder (Deuteronomy 21). In fact it deliberately combines and reverses them to make a point about Israel's hardness of heart, and its sequence follows the Torah's own order.
rows.arg:
P1 A conscious reworking of two texts that reverses their points and follows their sequence is not confusion. 
 P2 The Quran takes the cow's description from Numbers 19 and the murder from Deuteronomy 21, but turns the unsolved murder into a concealed one that the cow exposes, and makes the community guilty rather than innocent. It then moves, as Numbers does, from the cow to water from the rock. 
 ∴ The Quran's story is a deliberate, informed retelling.
rows.ev:
Numbers 19 describes a red heifer, without blemish, "on which a yoke has never come". The Quran's cow is a specific colour, flawless, "not trained to plough the earth or water the fields" (2:69-71).

 Deuteronomy 21:1-9 prescribes a heifer when a murdered man is found and the killer is unknown; the elders declare "our hands did not shed this blood". In the Quran, the community knows more than it admits: "you disputed over it, but Allah was to bring out what you were concealing" (2:72), and the cow's part restores the dead man to name his killer (2:73).

 The sequence. Numbers 19 (red heifer) is followed by Numbers 20 (water from the rock). The Quran follows the cow with: "then your hearts became hardened like stones, or even harder; for there are stones from which rivers gush forth" (2:74), echoing both the rock and Ezekiel's "heart of stone" (Ezek 36:26).

 Rabbinic links. Rabbinic tradition connects the red heifer with atonement for the golden calf, which the Quran mentions just before (2:51-54).

 No ashes. The Quran omits the ashes used for purification, because in its story the cow serves a single miraculous purpose.
rows.obj:
"Mixing two laws is still a mistake."
 The Quran isn't restating Torah law; it's narrating an episode in which Israel's stalling and concealment are exposed, and it draws on two Torah passages to do it, just as the NT writers merge OT texts (Mark 1:2-3 merges three).

 “The Quran mixes up the red heifer and the unsolved murder heifer.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer It uses both on purpose and reverses their points: the murder is concealed, not unknown, and the guilty community is exposed instead of cleared. It then follows Numbers' own sequence from the heifer to water from the rock (2:74). That is skilful allusion, not confusion.
rows.sum: The Quran combines Numbers 19's flawless, unyoked cow with Deuteronomy 21's murder ritual, reverses them (a concealed crime exposed), and follows Numbers' order from the heifer to water from the rock, ending with Ezekiel's "heart of stone".

title: Inheritance: the shares and the fractions (4:11-12)

rows.thesis: The inheritance verses are not mathematically flawed: Islamic law has always handled cases where shares exceed or fall short of the estate ('awl and radd). And the woman's "half share" applies only in some cases, tied to financial duties that fall on men.
rows.arg:
P1 A legal system that provides fixed shares and a rule for scaling them when they exceed the whole is complete, not erroneous. 
 P2 Islamic law scales shares proportionally ('awl) when they exceed one, and redistributes any remainder (radd) when they fall short. Women's shares depend on kinship, generation and financial obligation, and in many cases equal or exceed men's. 
 ∴ The inheritance law is coherent and just.
rows.ev:
'Awl. When fixed shares add up to more than the estate (for example a wife 1/8, two daughters 2/3, both parents 1/6 each), all shares are reduced proportionally. The Caliph Umar applied this with the Companions' agreement. Any modern law that guarantees several fixed claims must scale them when assets fall short, as in bankruptcy.

 Radd. When shares add up to less, the remainder returns to the heirs proportionally (or to residuary heirs).

 Why some men get double. Shares are set by (1) closeness of kinship, (2) generation (the younger generation, who have life ahead, often inherit more than the older), and (3) financial duty. Only in the third category does a son receive twice a daughter's share, because he must pay the dowry ( mahr ) and maintain his wife, children and often his parents and sisters, while a woman's wealth is entirely her own and she has no duty to spend it on the family.

 Women often equal or more. Uterine brothers and sisters inherit equally (4:12). A father and mother each get a sixth when there are children (4:11). In some cases a daughter receives more than a male relative, such as the deceased's brother.

title: The "severed aorta" (69:44-46)

rows.thesis: 69:44-46 says that if the Prophet ﷺ had fabricated revelation, Allah would have seized him and cut his aorta: a threat of swift death. The Prophet's later words about his aorta in pain were an idiom for severe pain, and he lived about four years after the poisoning.
rows.arg:
P1 A conditional threat ("if he had fabricated… We would have…") is not fulfilled unless the condition and its consequence both occur. 
 P2 The verse threatens swift death for fabrication; the Prophet ﷺ continued his mission for years after it and after the Khaybar poisoning; and his saying "I feel as if my aorta is being cut" uses "as if" to express pain. 
 ∴ The verse does not describe the Prophet's death and is not fulfilled against him.
rows.ev:
The verse. "Had he fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut his aorta ( al-watin ), and none of you could have shielded him" (69:44-47). It describes an immediate seizure and execution.

 The hadith. In his final illness, the Prophet ﷺ told Aisha: "I still feel the pain of the food I ate at Khaybar, and now I feel as if my aorta is being cut" (Bukhari 4428). Khaybar was in 7 AH; he died in 11 AH, about four years later, after the conquest of Mecca and the Farewell Pilgrimage.

 An idiom. "As if my aorta is being cut" is an Arabic expression for intense pain, like "my heart is breaking".

 The poisoning made him a martyr , as Ibn Mas'ud and others said, and he was not "seized by the right hand" in the act of fabricating.
rows.obj:
"He used the same word, watin , so he admitted the verse came true."
 He described a feeling ("as if"), not an event. And the verse's punishment is immediate seizure while fabricating, not a slow death years later after his mission was complete.

title: Quick answers to smaller objections

rows.thesis: Many objections disappear with a careful reading of the Arabic and the context.
rows.ev:
"Allah has no consort, so how could He have a son" (6:101) vs "had Allah wanted to take a son, He could have chosen" (39:4). 6:101 denies begetting , which would require a partner. 39:4 concerns taking ( ittakhadha , adopting), which is possible but which Allah did not do. No contradiction.

 "Allah is the best of plotters" (3:54). Makr used of Allah means turning the plotters' schemes against them (Lane's Lexicon ); the context is the plot against Jesus. The Bible goes further: God sends "a lying spirit" to entice Ahab (1 Kgs 22:20-23), and "God sends them a strong delusion so that they may believe what is false" (2 Thess 2:11).

 "Allah prays on the Prophet" (33:56). Salat from Allah means blessing and mercy (al-Khalil, al-Jawhari, Lane, Hans Wehr): "He sends salat on you… to bring you out of darkness into light" (33:43). Hebrew uses one verb, barak , both for God blessing Abraham (Gen 12:2) and people blessing God. Arabic Gospel manuscripts render "pray for those who persecute you" (Matt 5:44) as sallu 'ala .

 "An explanation of all things" (16:89). It means all things needed for guidance, as the context shows (16:64). The Torah is likewise called "an explanation of all things" (6:154; 7:145), and Jesus says the Spirit will guide "into all truth" (John 16:13), not into physics.

 "First of the Muslims" (said of Muhammad, Moses and others) means first of their time or community (Tabari).

 "Allah forgives all sins" (39:53) vs "Allah does not forgive shirk" (4:48). 39:53 is about those who repent; 4:48 about those who die associating partners with Him.

 "The worst of creatures" (98:6) describes the final state of those who reject clear proof, not ethnicity.

 "The Messiah" in 9:31. "They took their rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah, and the Messiah ": the grammar ( al-Masiha , accusative) puts the Messiah with the rabbis and monks as creatures wrongly taken as lords.

 Did Jesus know the unseen (3:49)? Telling people what they ate and stored was a sign revealed to him (5:110). Jesus himself says: "You know what is within me and I do not know what is within You" (5:116). Allah reveals some of the unseen to chosen messengers (72:26-27). Jesus is a "sign" ( 'alam ) of the Hour (43:61), not one who knows its time; only Allah knows it (31:34).

 Thamud's chronology. The Quran gives an order (Noah, then 'Ad, then Thamud, 7:69-74) but no dates. Sargon II's inscription (715 BCE) records the Tamudi, which attests them; it does not date their beginning.

 Revelation in stages (25:32) was to strengthen the Prophet's heart and answer events as they arose.

 "His people called him bewitched" : every prophet was called a sorcerer or madman (51:52).

section_title: Objections about the Prophet ﷺ and his religion
title: The experience of revelation was not epilepsy or possession

rows.thesis: The physical signs that accompanied revelation (sweating, heaviness, the sound like a bell) do not match epilepsy, and they parallel what the Bible says happened to prophets like Daniel. The Prophet's ﷺ faculties were intact to the end, and Satan does not preach against Satan.
rows.arg:
P1 Epilepsy and possession produce confusion, loss of awareness and, over time, decline; they do not produce a coherent book recited back exactly. 
 P2 During revelation the Prophet ﷺ remained aware, then recited the revealed text exactly; he showed no decline over 23 years; and biblical prophets had similar overwhelming experiences. 
 ∴ The revelation experience was not epilepsy or possession.
rows.ev:
What happened. Aisha: "I saw him receiving revelation on a very cold day, and when it ended his forehead was dripping with sweat" (Bukhari 2). His face reddened and he breathed heavily (Bukhari 4602). The Quran calls it "a weighty word" (73:5). He said it sometimes came " like the ringing of a bell" (Bukhari 2), a simile for its intensity, and sometimes the angel came in the form of a man, which was easier.

 Not epilepsy. W. Montgomery Watt ( Muhammad at Mecca , p. 57) rejects the epilepsy theory: epilepsy causes degeneration, while Muhammad kept full mental vigour to the end; such physical accompaniments neither prove nor disprove revelation.

 Ibn Khaldun explains the strain as the prophetic soul being lifted momentarily from human to angelic perception.

 Biblical parallels. Daniel, seeing the angel: "no strength was left in me… I fell into a deep sleep on my face… I have no strength, and no breath is left in me" (Dan 10:8-17). Jacob was wrestled and his hip dislocated (Gen 32:24-25); Zechariah was terrified and struck mute (Luke 1:12, 20).

 The first revelation. Gabriel pressed him at Hira (Bukhari 3), as angels overwhelmed Daniel. Later reports say Gabriel reassured him: "O Muhammad, you are the Messenger of Allah" (al-Bidaya 3/21), and further comfort followed (Surah al-Duha; Bukhari 1125).

 Satan's work? Abu Lahab's wife taunted that his "devil" had left him. Jesus too was accused of Beelzebub (Mark 3:22), and answered that Satan does not cast out Satan (see Dilemmas for Christians ).
rows.obj:
"Even if not epilepsy, it could be a psychological condition."
 A condition that produced, over 23 years, a text that its hostile audience couldn't match, a coherent law and a successful community, while its subject remained lucid and was trusted by everyone as al-Amin, is not like any known disorder.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Muhammad had seizures, foamed at the mouth and thought he was possessed.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer The sources say he sweated, felt heaviness and heard a sound "like a bell", and then recited exact verses. Watt rejects epilepsy because it degrades the mind, while his remained sharp. Daniel fell on his face breathless before an angel; no one calls him epileptic.

title: Allah is not Hubal or a moon god

rows.thesis: Hubal was a specific imported idol whom the Prophet ﷺ opposed by name; the moon-god theory has no evidence; and Allah is the name Arab Christians and Jews used for the God of Abraham.

title: The Kaaba and Hajj restore Abraham's worship

section_title: Objections about the Prophet ﷺ and his religion
title: The "Satanic verses" story is not authentic

rows.thesis: The story that the Prophet ﷺ praised the pagan goddesses (the gharaniq incident) comes only through broken chains, and it was rejected by the major scholars of hadith and tafsir.
rows.arg:
P1 A historical report is accepted only if it has a connected chain of reliable narrators. 
 P2 Every chain of the gharaniq story is mursal (missing the Companion) or otherwise broken; scholars from Ibn Kathir to al-Albani rejected it. 
 ∴ The story is not established.
rows.ev:
The chains. All versions are mursal or come through weak narrators; none reaches a Companion who witnessed the event. Al-Albani's treatise Nasb al-Majaniq li-Nasf Qissat al-Gharaniq goes through every chain and shows each one fails.

 The scholars. Ibn Kathir says all its chains are mursal and he has not seen it with a connected sound chain. It was rejected by al-Baghawi, al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari, al-Qadi 'Iyad, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Hazm. Al-Razi reports that Ibn Ishaq called it a fabrication of heretics.

 The Quran's own context. The surah in question (al-Najm) condemns the goddesses outright: "they are nothing but names you have named" (53:23). The Prophet ﷺ is protected from adding to revelation (69:44-47).

 Even if one took the story seriously, 22:52 says Satan's insertions are cancelled by Allah, which means the Quran was corrected and preserved, not corrupted.
rows.obj:
"Early historians like Tabari and Ibn Sa'd record it, so it must be true."
 Tabari recorded many reports with their chains, explicitly warning that the responsibility lies with the narrators. A report's appearance in a collection is not a verdict on its authenticity.

Your opponent says
 “Your own historians record that Muhammad praised the pagan goddesses.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer They record a story whose every chain is broken, and the leading hadith scholars rejected it. The same surah calls the goddesses "nothing but names". It fails the standard Muslims use for every report.

section_title: Objections about the Prophet ﷺ and his religion
title: Zaynab and Zayd

rows.thesis: The Prophet's ﷺ marriage to Zaynab after her divorce from Zayd was commanded to end the pre-Islamic custom of treating adopted sons as blood sons. The Prophet had urged Zayd to keep his wife, and Zaynab was his own cousin whom he could have married years earlier.
rows.arg:
P1 A charge of lust must explain why the Prophet ﷺ himself arranged Zaynab's first marriage to Zayd and urged him to keep her. 
 P2 Zaynab was the Prophet's cousin; he arranged her marriage to Zayd; when the marriage failed he told Zayd "keep your wife and fear Allah" (33:37); and the Quran explains the purpose of the later marriage: to abolish the adoption taboo (33:4-5, 37). 
 ∴ The marriage was a legal reform, not a scandal.
rows.ev:
Background. Zayd ibn Haritha chose to stay with the Prophet ﷺ rather than return to his own father, and was adopted under pre-Islamic custom. The Prophet ﷺ married him to Zaynab bint Jahsh, a noble woman of Quraysh and the Prophet's own cousin, whom he had known all her life.

 He urged the marriage to continue. "You said to the one whom Allah had favoured and you had favoured: keep your wife and fear Allah" (33:37). Zayd divorced her by his own choice.

 Double standard. David took Bathsheba and arranged her husband's death (2 Sam 11), and the NT still calls him a prophet (Acts 2:30).

section_title: Objections about the Prophet ﷺ and his religion
title: Other objections about the Prophet ﷺ

rows.thesis: Several further charges collapse when the sources are read in full.
rows.ev:
"He worshipped idols before Islam." The report about meat offered to Zayd ibn 'Amr (Bukhari 3826; 5499) comes in another version in which both refused it, and in any case it was before revelation. The Bible says Solomon built shrines to idols during his prophethood (1 Kgs 11:4-9).

 "Expel the Jews and Christians from Arabia" (Muslim 1767). It concerns the Hijaz and its holy sites, after the hostilities at Khaybar. Jews remained under treaty (Muslim 1551) until Umar relocated them, and the Prophet ﷺ died with his armour pawned to a Jew for barley (Bukhari 2916). 60:8 commands kindness to peaceful non-Muslims.

The chain is weak: 'Amr al-Bikali is not known to have heard from Ibn Mas'ud, and Ibn Mas'ud himself said, "I was not with the Prophet on the Night of the Jinn" (Muslim 450). Yarkabun in Arabic idiom means crowding closely, as in 72:19, where the jinn "almost became a mass around him" ( libadan ) to hear the Quran.

 "Babies in Hell" (Musnad Ahmad: the girl buried alive and the one who buried her are in the Fire). Ibn 'Abd al-Barr explains it as an answer about a specific case. title: Hadith criticism is rigorous, even about the Sahih collections

rows.thesis: Muslim scholars criticised and rejected weak reports, including a narration in Sahih Muslim, by examining both chains and content. That honesty is why a critic cannot treat every report as "what Islam teaches".

title: Abu Hurayra's large number of hadith

rows.thesis: Abu Hurayra narrated many hadith because he devoted himself to the Prophet's ﷺ company and teaching, the Prophet prayed for his memory, and other young Companions also narrated thousands.
rows.arg:
P1 The number of reports a Companion narrated depends on how long he lived after the Prophet, how much he devoted himself to learning, and how much he taught. 
 P2 Abu Hurayra lived with the Prophet ﷺ full-time, had his memory blessed by the Prophet's prayer, and taught for decades in Medina; other junior Companions like Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas also narrated thousands. 
 ∴ His number of narrations is not suspicious.
rows.ev:
Devotion. Abu Hurayra said: "My brothers among the Muhajirun were busy in the markets and the Ansar with their property, while I stayed with the Messenger of Allah to fill my stomach" (Bukhari 118). He was one of the People of the Suffa who lived at the mosque.

 The prayer for memory. He spread his cloak, the Prophet ﷺ spoke, and he never forgot afterward (Bukhari 119).

 Others. Ibn Umar has about 2,600 narrations and Ibn Abbas, who was only nine to fourteen when the Prophet died, about 1,700. Jonathan Brown ( Hadith , pp. 18-19) notes that junior Companions who lived long and taught widely narrated the most.

 Counting. The 5,300 figure counts every chain separately; the number of distinct reports is far smaller.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Abu Hurayra was with the Prophet for only three years but narrated more than anyone, so he must have invented hadith.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer He spent those years at the Prophet's side full-time (Bukhari 118), the Prophet prayed for his memory (Bukhari 119), and he taught for decades after. Ibn Abbas was a child and still narrated 1,700. The 5,300 counts chains, not distinct reports.

title: The "assassinations" attributed to the Prophet ﷺ

rows.thesis: The killings critics cite are either fabricated (Asma bint Marwan), weakly transmitted and contradicting known law (Umm Qirfa), or were punishments for murder and acts of war (Abu 'Afak, Miqyas, al-Huwayrith), not for mere words or poetry.
rows.arg:
P1 A charge must rest on an authentic report and an accurate account of the reason. 
 P2 The Asma bint Marwan story is fabricated; the Umm Qirfa story is weak and contradicts the ban on killing women and mutilation; the others were combatants or murderers. 
 ∴ There is no authentic case of the Prophet ﷺ killing someone merely for criticising him.
rows.ev:
Asma bint Marwan. The story comes through Muhammad ibn al-Hajjaj al-Lakhmi, whom Bukhari, Ibn Ma'in and al-Daraqutni called a liar; al-Albani graded it fabricated ( mawdu' ).

 Umm Qirfa. Her brutal killing is reported through an interrupted chain with weak narrators (Ibn Humayd, Salama). Al-Dhahabi calls it munkar . It contradicts the Prophet's explicit bans on mutilation and on killing women.

 Abu 'Afak. Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Kathir and al-Zurqani describe him as inciting war against the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims; the issue was incitement to fight, not poetry.

 Miqyas ibn Subaba killed the Ansari who had paid him blood money for his brother, then apostatised and fled. His execution was retaliation ( qisas ) for murder.

 Al-Huwayrith attacked the Prophet's daughters as they fled Mecca and fought the Muslims.

 The principle. Aisha: "The Messenger of Allah never took revenge for himself" (Bukhari 3560). At the conquest of Mecca he pardoned almost everyone who had persecuted him for 20 years.

Your opponent says
 “Muhammad had poets killed for mocking him.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer The Asma bint Marwan story is fabricated by a known liar; Abu 'Afak was inciting war; Miqyas was a murderer. Aisha said he never took revenge for himself, and he pardoned all of Mecca.

title: "The Prophet ﷺ attempted suicide"

rows.thesis: The passage in Bukhari 6982 about the Prophet ﷺ going to throw himself from a mountain is an unconnected addition by al-Zuhri ("it reached us that…"), not part of Aisha's connected narration.
rows.arg:
P1 A statement is a hadith of the Prophet ﷺ only if it has a connected chain to him. 
 P2 In Bukhari 6982, the mountain passage is introduced by al-Zuhri with "it reached us ( balaghana )", with no chain; Aisha's connected narration ends before it. 
 ∴ The suicide claim is not an authenticated hadith.
rows.ev:
In Bukhari 6982, after Aisha's account of the first revelation and the pause in revelation, the text continues "and the Prophet ﷺ was so grieved, as it reached us , that he went several times to throw himself from the mountain tops…". Ibn Hajar notes this is among al-Zuhri's balaghat , unconnected reports.

 Bukhari includes it inside a longer narration but does not present it as a sound hadith in its own right; the authentic version of the first revelation (Bukhari 3; 4953) does not contain it.

 Even in the report, Gabriel appears each time and reassures him, and he does not harm himself.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Sahih Bukhari says Muhammad tried to kill himself, so he doubted his prophethood.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer The passage is al-Zuhri's "it reached us", without a chain, attached to Aisha's narration. Aisha's own connected report in Bukhari 3 doesn't contain it. Unchained hearsay isn't a hadith.

title: Other hadith objections answered

rows.thesis: Most remaining objections come from weak reports, reports not from the Prophet ﷺ, or misreadings.
rows.ev:
The well of Buda'ah (Abu Dawud 67). The narrator 'Ubaydullah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Rafi' is unknown. The principle in the hadith is that water stays pure unless its smell, colour or taste changes. Al-Khattabi explains that the Companions never threw filth in; rain washed refuse into the well from the surrounding ground. Islam forbids urinating in standing water.

 "The Black Stone expiates sins" (Tirmidhi). The narrator 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib's memory became confused, and Jarir heard from him late; the chain also has a break (Ibn 'Ubayd from his father).

 'Ali burning heretics. Reports differ (some say he burned their house or their corpses after execution). Ibn Abbas condemned it, quoting the Prophet's ﷺ ban: "Do not punish with Allah's punishment [fire]" (Bukhari 3017). At most it was 'Ali's error, corrected by a Companion with the Prophet's ruling.

 "Allah will give each Muslim a Jew or Christian as ransom from Hell" (Muslim 2767). Every person has a place in Paradise and a place in Hell; the believer's place in Hell goes to the disbeliever who earned it. Al-Nawawi explains it as ransom ( fida' ), not transferring sins.

 "If you did not sin, Allah would replace you with people who sin and seek forgiveness" (Muslim 2749). It is about Allah's love of repentance, not encouraging sin. Compare Luke 15:7: "there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons."

 Moses' stone running off with his clothes; stones speaking. The Bible has stones that "cry out" (Luke 19:40; Hab 2:11) and a stone that "has heard all the words of the LORD" (Josh 24:27).

 "Monkeys stoning an adulterous monkey" (Bukhari 3849). It is the observation of 'Amr ibn Maymun, a Successor, before he became Muslim, not a saying of the Prophet ﷺ; Ibn 'Abd al-Barr says the longer version has weak chains.

 "Father, forgive them, for they know not" (Bukhari 3477). The Prophet ﷺ narrated a prophet saying this while wiping blood from his face, so it is not about a crucifixion. Qadi 'Iyad says it describes the Prophet himself at Uhud; 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr attributes the words to Noah. Luke 23:34, where Jesus says it, is missing from P75, the first hand of Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and Bezae.

 Cousin marriage. It is permitted, not required. Alan Bittles, the leading researcher on consanguinity, estimates the added risk of birth defects for first cousins at a few per cent, comparable to that of mothers over 40, who are not banned from having children.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Islam says water polluted by menstrual cloths and dog flesh is pure (the well of Buda'ah).”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer The narrator is unknown, the Companions didn't throw filth in (rain washed it from the ground, per al-Khattabi), and the rule is that water becomes impure when its smell, colour or taste changes. Islam forbids even urinating in standing water.

title: Women's intellect, testimony and status

rows.thesis: The hadith about women's "deficiency in intellect and religion" refers to reduced legal burdens, was said lightly in praise of women's persuasive power, and Islamic law weighs testimony by reliability, not sex. Women were among Islam's leading scholars.
rows.arg:
P1 A text must be read with its wording, tone and the law it refers to. 
 P2 The hadith (Bukhari 304; 1462) explains the "deficiency" as the two-woman rule in commercial contracts and the exemption from prayer and fasting during menstruation, both lighter burdens, and it begins with praise of women's ability to sway "a resolute man's" mind. 
 ∴ The hadith does not teach that women are inferior in intelligence or worth.
rows.ev:
The text. The Prophet ﷺ told a group of women: "I have not seen anyone deficient in intellect and religion more able to take away the reason of a resolute man than one of you." When a woman asked what the deficiency was, he explained: the testimony of two women in place of one man (2:282), and not praying or fasting during menstruation. Both are legal concessions. The tone is gentle teasing, and one of the women who questioned him is described as "highly intelligent" ( jazla , Muslim 79).

 
 Tap to enlarge Sahih al-Bukhari 1462: the hadith on women's "deficiency" in its full context 
 
 "Naqs" means reduction. The Quran uses the same root for "reducing the land from its borders" (13:41); it means a smaller share, not a defect.

 The two-woman rule is limited to commercial contracts, and the verse gives the reason: "so that if one errs, the other can remind her" (2:282), reflecting women's limited involvement in trade at the time. Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim held that the purpose is reliability, so a more credible woman's testimony can outweigh a man's, and in many matters a woman's testimony alone is accepted.

 Women scholars. The Companions brought their hardest questions to Aisha (Tirmidhi 3883). Al-Dhahabi lists over a hundred women hadith narrators, and he said no woman was ever accused of lying in hadith.

 Christian comparison. Paul: "women should keep silent in the churches… if they want to learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home" (1 Cor 14:34-35). Tertullian called woman "the devil's gateway".
rows.ar:
فَإِن لَّمْ يَكُونَا رَجُلَيْنِ فَرَجُلٌ وَامْرَأَتَانِ مِمَّن تَرْضَوْنَ مِنَ الشُّهَدَاءِ أَن تَضِلَّ إِحْدَاهُمَا فَتُذَكِّرَ إِحْدَاهُمَا الْأُخْرَىٰ
 2:282
rows.obj:
"Two women for one man still says women are less reliable."
 The verse gives a practical reason (one may remind the other), applies only to financial contracts, and the scholars made reliability, not sex, the criterion. In matters where women had expertise, their testimony alone was accepted.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Islam says women are deficient in intelligence.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer The Prophet ﷺ explained exactly what he meant: two legal concessions, the commercial testimony rule and exemption from prayer during menses. He said it while praising women's power to sway a resolute man. Aisha was the person the Companions consulted on their hardest questions.
rows.sum: The "deficiency" hadith refers to two legal concessions and was said in light praise; naqs means reduction (13:41); the two-witness rule is for contracts, with a stated practical reason; and Aisha and over a hundred women narrators shaped Islamic scholarship.

title: 4:34 and domestic violence

rows.thesis: 4:34 allows, as a last resort after admonition and separation, a symbolic strike that may not cause pain, mark or injury. The Prophet ﷺ never struck a woman, condemned men who did, and the jurists allowed a wife to divorce and claim redress if harmed. The hadith "a man will not be asked why he beat his wife" is weak.

title: Polygyny: limited, conditioned and discouraged

rows.thesis: Islam took unlimited polygamy and limited it to four, conditioned on justice, and the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools recommended keeping to one. A wife may stipulate in her contract that her husband take no second wife.
rows.arg:
P1 A law should be judged by what it replaced and the conditions it imposed. 
 P2 Pre-Islamic Arabs had unlimited wives; the Quran limited it to four and said "if you fear you will not be just, then one" (4:3), adding "you will never be able to be perfectly just" (4:129). 
 ∴ The Quran's law is a restriction, not a licence.
rows.ev:
The limit. A man who became Muslim with eight wives was told to keep four (Abu Dawud 2241).

 The condition. "Marry those that please you, two, three or four; but if you fear you will not be just, then one" (4:3). "A man who has two wives and favours one will come on the Day of Resurrection with one side leaning" (Abu Dawud 2133).

 Recommended one. Al-Shafi'i, Ibn Qudama, al-Buhuti, al-Nawawi and al-Mawardi recommend keeping to one wife.

 
 Tap to enlarge Classical fiqh: al-Shafi'i preferred limiting oneself to one wife (4:3) 
 
 The wife's right. Imam Ahmad's school allows a wife to stipulate in the marriage contract that her husband will take no other wife, and the stipulation is binding.

 The Prophet's marriages were mostly to widows and for social or political reasons: his marriage to Juwayriya led the Companions to free a hundred families of her tribe.

 The Bible has no limit: Solomon had 700 wives (1 Kgs 11:3), and God "gave" David Saul's wives (2 Sam 12:8). See Morality in the Bible & the Church .

title: Slavery: regulated toward abolition

rows.thesis: Islam inherited a world in which slavery was universal. It closed most routes into slavery, opened many routes out, made freeing slaves an act of worship and expiation, punished abuse by freeing the slave, and forbade forced intercourse.
rows.arg:
P1 A law in a world where slavery was universal should be judged by whether it reduced and humanised it. 
 P2 Islam forbade enslaving free people, encouraged releasing prisoners, required granting slaves contracts to buy their freedom, allocated zakat to freeing them, made freeing slaves the expiation for many sins, and freed a slave whose master struck him. 
 ∴ Islamic law pushed steadily against slavery.
rows.ev:
Routes in closed. Selling a free person is a major sin (Bukhari 2227). Captives may be freed as a favour or for ransom (47:4); at Badr the ransom for some literate captives was teaching Muslims to read. At the conquest of Mecca he said: "Go, you are free." Ibn Qudama: the elderly, sick, blind and monks may not be captured.

 Routes out. Slaves who ask for a contract of freedom must be granted one (24:33). Zakat funds freeing slaves (9:60). Freeing a slave is the expiation for manslaughter (4:92), breaking oaths (5:89), and other sins, and the "steep path" to righteousness (90:13).

 Protection. "Whoever slaps or beats his slave, his expiation is to free him" (Muslim 1657). When Abu Mas'ud struck his slave, the Prophet ﷺ said "Allah has more power over you than you have over him", and he freed him (Muslim 1659). "Feed them from what you eat and clothe them from what you wear" (Bukhari 30). Among the Prophet's last words: "the prayer, and those your right hands possess."

 No forced intercourse. Al-Shafi'i: "no one can be compelled to it" ( al-Umm ). Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim held that forcing a slave woman into intercourse is a form of mutilation that frees her; al-Halimi said if she dislikes his touch he must not touch her without her permission and must sell her if she wishes. Jonathan Brown's Slavery and Islam discusses these rulings.

 The Bible permits buying slaves from the nations as permanent property (Lev 25:44-46), allows beating a slave who survives "a day or two" without penalty because "he is his money" (Exod 21:20-21), and the NT tells slaves to obey even harsh masters (1 Pet 2:18).

 24:33 
 فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ
 90:13
rows.obj:
"Why not abolish it outright?"
 No society abolished slavery until the 19th century. Islam did what was possible in the 7th century: close the main sources, open many exits, and tie freeing slaves to worship. The direction was toward freedom.

title: Non-Muslims under Islamic rule

rows.thesis: Jews and Christians under Islam were protected, kept their courts and churches, and often welcomed Muslim rule over Byzantine persecution. Historians agree they fared far better than minorities under medieval Christian rule.
rows.arg:
P1 A religion's treatment of minorities is judged by the historical record. 
 P2 Christian sources of the 7th century describe Arab rule as a relief; Muslims returned jizya when they could not protect; Jews fled Christian Spain to Muslim lands; and historians such as Mark Cohen find Jewish life under Islam far more secure than under Christianity. 
 ∴ Islam's record with minorities was good by the standards of its time and better than its rivals'.

Christian testimony. Isho'yahb III, patriarch of the Church of the East in the 7th century: the Arabs "are not enemies to Christianity… they honour our priests and saints and give gifts to churches and monasteries."

 
 Tap to enlarge Isho'yahb III (Church of the East, 7th c.): the Arabs "are not enemies to Christianity… they honour our priests" 
 
 Relief from Byzantium. Michael the Syrian recorded that God sent the sons of Ishmael to free them from the Romans; Christoph Baumer describes Syriac Christians seeing Arab rule as relief from Byzantine persecution.

 
 Tap to enlarge Christoph Baumer, The Church of the East : Syriac Christians saw Arab rule as relief from Byzantium

 Tap to enlarge Coptic Synaxarium: 'Amr returned Pope Benjamin after 13 years in hiding and restored the churches 
 
 Hims. When Abu 'Ubayda had to withdraw from Hims before the Byzantine army, he returned the jizya to its Christians because he could no longer protect them; they prayed for the Muslims' return (al-Baladhuri; T.W. Arnold, The Preaching of Islam ).

 Jews. Mark R. Cohen ( Under Crescent and Cross ) concludes that Jews under Islam had their own courts, were integrated economically, rarely faced forced conversion, and kept no collective memory of persecution comparable to Christian Europe. After 1492, Jews expelled from Spain found refuge in the Ottoman Empire and North Africa.

title: Banu Qurayza

rows.thesis: The Banu Qurayza broke their treaty and sided with the besieging army during the Battle of the Trench. Their fate was decided by an arbiter they chose themselves, according to the law of their own Torah, and only their fighting men were executed.

title: Hijab and modesty

rows.thesis: The hijab is a command to cover the head and body in public, shared with Jewish and Christian tradition, and its stated purpose is dignity and protection from harassment.
rows.arg:
P1 The meaning of the command is fixed by the Arabic and the context. 
 P2 Khimar means a head covering (Lisan al-'Arab), and 24:31 tells women to draw it over their chests; 33:59 gives the purpose, "so they will be recognised and not harassed".

title: The Prophet ﷺ did not use revelation for personal gain

rows.thesis: Critics say revelations conveniently served the Prophet ﷺ. His lifestyle shows the opposite: he lived in poverty while ruling Arabia, forbade charity to his own family, and the Quran rebuked him.
rows.arg:
P1 A man who invented revelation for personal benefit would live in comfort and spare himself criticism. 
 P2 The Prophet ﷺ slept on a reed mat, gave away wealth, forbade his family from receiving charity, prayed until his feet swelled, and recited verses rebuking himself. 
 ∴ The "convenient revelation" theory doesn't fit his life.
rows.ev:
Poverty. Umar wept seeing the marks of the reed mat on the Prophet's side while kings slept on silk (Ibn Majah 4153). He said he would not want gold the size of Mount Uhud to remain with him more than three days (Bukhari 6444). He died with his armour pawned for barley (Bukhari 2916).

 Worship. He prayed at night until his feet swelled, saying "Should I not be a grateful servant?" (Bukhari 4836).

 His family barred from charity. Zakat may not be given to the Prophet's family (Muslim 1072).

 Self-rebuke. "He frowned and turned away because the blind man came to him" (80:1-2); "Allah pardon you, why did you give them leave?" (9:43); "it is not for a prophet to take captives…" (8:67).

 Refused worldly offers. The Quraysh offered him kingship, wealth and the most beautiful women to stop preaching; he refused.

section_title: Aisha's age, 65:4 and the end of Surah at-Tawbah
title: The authentic reports put Aisha's age at marriage at nine

rows.thesis: The age of six at the contract and nine at consummation is narrated through several independent chains and was agreed upon by classical scholars. The "she was 19" arguments rely on weak or misread reports.
rows.arg:
P1 An honest defence must start from the authentic evidence, not the convenient one. 
 P2 The reports giving six and nine come through multiple independent chains, including one without Hisham ibn 'Urwa; Ibn Hazm, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr reported no disagreement; the counter-arguments rely on a weak report about Asma's age, a misreading of the Uhud reports, and a confused report about Fatima. 
 ∴ Aisha was nine at consummation; the defence must address that, not deny it.
rows.ev:
Multiple chains. Bukhari 5133, 5134 and 5158 (through Hisham ibn 'Urwa); Muslim 1422 through al-A'mash from Ibrahim from al-Aswad, with no Hisham in the chain; and through Yahya ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Hatib (Abu Dawud 4937).

 Hisham's reliability. Al-Dhahabi calls him "a proof, an imam" and rejects the claim that his memory became confused ( Mizan 4/301). Ibn al-Salah and al-Nawawi note that the narrations in Bukhari and Muslim come from his sound period.

 Agreement. Ibn Hazm said it was "without any difference"; Ibn Kathir "there is no disagreement among people"; Ibn 'Abd al-Barr "I know of no one who differed". Ahmad Shakir called claims to the contrary fabricated.

 The counter-arguments fail. The report that Asma was ten years older comes only from Ibn Abi al-Zinad, born after Aisha's death, without a chain, and he is weak per Ibn Ma'in, Ahmad and al-Nasa'i. At Uhud, Aisha carried water as a helper, not as a combatant, so the age limit for fighters doesn't apply. The report about Fatima's age mixes two inconsistent dates. Aisha's memory of Surah al-Qamar's revelation ("I was a playful young girl, jariya ") fits a girl of about four or five, and children like Ibn Abbas narrated events from age three. The idea that Arabs counted age from puberty has no basis and would make Asma 110.
rows.obj:
"Why not accept the 19 theory? It solves the problem."
 Because it is false history, and an apologetic built on weak evidence collapses as soon as an informed opponent checks it. The strong answer is the context argument below.
rows.rebut:
Your opponent says
 “Many Muslims say Aisha was really 19, so even Muslims are embarrassed.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Some do, but the evidence for six and nine comes through several independent chains, and classical scholars reported no disagreement. The real question is whether the marriage was wrong in its context, and the evidence says it was not.

section_title: Aisha's age, 65:4 and the end of Surah at-Tawbah
title: The marriage judged by its own time, and by its outcome

rows.thesis: Marriage soon after puberty was normal across the ancient and medieval world, including Christian, Jewish, Persian and Roman law. The marriage was consummated after Aisha reached physical maturity, with her consent and her family's, it was never criticised by the Prophet's enemies, and she became one of the greatest scholars of Islam.
rows.arg:
P1 Moral judgement of a historical act must account for the norms of its time and the actual circumstances. 
 P2 Marriage around puberty was normal everywhere; Aisha was already engaged before; the consummation was delayed until maturity; she consented; no enemy of the Prophet objected; and she flourished. 
 ∴ The marriage was not immoral in its context.
rows.ev:
Universal norm. 

 
 Sasanian Persian law expected girls to marry from nine and consummate by twelve ( Encyclopaedia Iranica , "Children").

 Roman law set the minimum age for girls at twelve; medieval canon law did the same, with betrothal from seven.

 Geza Vermes thought Mary was likely about twelve when betrothed to Joseph; the Protevangelium of James says she was given to an elderly Joseph at twelve. Augustine's fiancée was about ten ( Confessions 6.13).

 In the 19th century, the age of consent in many US states was ten or even seven, and some US states still have no minimum marriage age.

 Historians such as Neil Postman ( The Disappearance of Childhood ) show that "childhood" as an extended protected stage is a modern idea; Gluckman and Hanson ( Mismatch ) note that physical puberty and social maturity coincided historically.

 
 Maturity. 

 
 Puberty varies widely: the average range is about 9-14, and medical references give menarche from 9 to 17. Hot climates are associated with earlier onset. Al-Shafi'i said he saw girls in Yemen reach puberty at nine, and a grandmother aged 21 (al-Bayhaqi).

 Aisha said, "When a girl reaches nine, she is a woman" (Tirmidhi). She described her illness before the marriage and her hair growing back (Bukhari 3894). Jonathan Brown ( Misquoting Muhammad ) explains that consummation took place only after physical maturity; contract and consummation were separate stages.

 
 Tap to enlarge Jonathan Brown, Misquoting Muhammad : consummation only after physical maturity; contract is not consummation 
 Tap to enlarge Gray's Anatomy , pre- and postnatal development: growth and pubertal timing vary 
 
 Al-Dawudi (quoted by Qadi 'Iyad): Aisha had reached good physical maturity, and a girl who cannot bear marriage should not be given in marriage.

 
 Consent and outcome. 

 
 Aisha was already engaged to Jubayr ibn Mut'im before the Prophet ﷺ proposed, through Khawla bint Hakim; her parents agreed.

 When the Quran gave the Prophet's wives the choice to leave him (33:28-29), Aisha answered first: "I choose Allah, His Messenger and the Home of the Hereafter" (Bukhari 4785).

 The Prophet ﷺ let a girl annul a marriage her father arranged without her consent (al-Nasa'i 3269), and Islamic law's principle "no harm" ( la darar ) forbids a marriage that harms the girl.

 No enemy of the Prophet, among the Quraysh, the hypocrites or the Jews of Medina, who attacked him on every point, objected to this marriage.

 Aisha became the leading scholar of her generation, narrating over 2,000 hadith; the Companions brought her their hardest questions.
rows.obj:
"Morality is timeless; it was wrong then too."
 Islam agrees that harm is always wrong, which is why the law forbids harmful marriages. But age norms for marriage are not timeless; they track physical maturity and social structure. If marriage at 12-14 is timelessly evil, then most of humanity's ancestors, including Mary according to Christian tradition, were in evil marriages.


 "Should Muslims follow this today?"
 Islamic law requires maturity, the absence of harm and, for a mature woman, her consent, and allows states to set minimum ages to prevent harm. Following the Prophet ﷺ does not mean reproducing the social age norms of 7th-century Arabia.

 “Muhammad married a child; no context excuses that.”

Aisha's marriage was consummated after maturity, she chose to stay when given the choice (Bukhari 4785), no enemy of the Prophet objected, and she became the greatest scholar of her generation.

title: 65:4: "those who have not menstruated"

rows.thesis: 65:4 sets the waiting period after divorce for women who do not menstruate. It covers women whose periods are delayed or absent for any reason, and does not authorise intercourse with prepubescent girls.
rows.arg:
P1 A verse about the waiting period after divorce regulates divorce; it does not set permissions for intercourse, which are governed by other rules (maturity and no harm). 
 P2 Puberty begins well before first menstruation, and some women never menstruate or have irregular cycles; the verse gives all of them a fixed three-month period. 
 ∴ 65:4 does not imply sex with prepubescent children.
rows.ev:
The verse. "Those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you are in doubt, their waiting period is three months, and [also for] those who have not menstruated" (65:4).

 Biology. Puberty begins around ages 8-13 with physical changes, while menarche usually comes later, around 12-13, and can be delayed into the late teens. Some women have primary amenorrhoea (never menstruating) due to medical conditions, or very irregular cycles.

 The law elsewhere. Consummation requires the ability to bear it without harm; the jurists ruled that a girl who cannot bear it may not be given to her husband. The waiting period also applies after the death of a husband even without consummation, so it does not imply intercourse.

title: The end of Surah at-Tawbah (9:128-129)

rows.thesis: Zayd ibn Thabit found the last two verses of Surah at-Tawbah written only with Abu Khuzayma, but they were memorised by many Companions; written proof was an extra check. The verses appear in first-century manuscripts.
rows.arg:

title: The Quran itself requires the Sunnah (against Quranists)

rows.thesis: The Quran refers to revelation outside its text, commands obedience to the Messenger separately, calls him its explainer, and cannot be practised without the Sunnah. Rejecting hadith therefore contradicts the Quran.
rows.arg:
P1 If the Quran mentions revelations that are not in it, and makes the Prophet ﷺ the explainer of the Quran, then revelation outside the Quran exists and binds Muslims. 
 P2 The Quran refers to promises and commands not recorded in it (3:124; 2:143; 2:187), distinguishes "the Book and the Wisdom", and says the Prophet was sent "to explain to people what was sent down to them" (16:44). 
 ∴ The Sunnah is revelation alongside the Quran, and the Quranist position contradicts the Quran.
rows.ev:
Revelation not in the Quran. "Is it not sufficient that your Lord reinforces you with three thousand angels?" (3:124), a promise recorded in no earlier verse. "We did not make the qibla you used to face except to know who follows the Messenger" (2:143), but no verse ever commanded the earlier qibla. "Allah knows you used to deceive yourselves" about intercourse at night in Ramadan (2:187), a prohibition never stated in the Quran.

 The Book and the Wisdom. "He teaches them the Book and the Wisdom" (2:129; 62:2); the two are distinct.

 The explainer. "We sent down to you the Reminder so that you may explain to people what was sent down to them" (16:44). "Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; whatever he forbids you, refrain" (59:7). "Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah" (4:80).

 Practice. How to pray, the zakat rates and thresholds, the rites of Hajj, and even the seven modes of recitation are known only from the Sunnah.

 Same transmitters. The Quran and the hadith were carried by the same Companions and their students; rejecting their reliability for one undermines the other.

 The clarity dilemma. Quranists say the Quran is clear on its own. Yet the overwhelming majority of Muslims across 1,400 years understood it to require the Sunnah. If a "clear" book was misunderstood by almost everyone, it was not clear in the Quranist sense.

وَأَنزَلْنَا إِلَيْكَ الذِّكْرَ لِتُبَيِّنَ لِلنَّاسِ مَا نُزِّلَ إِلَيْهِمْ

 59:7

title: Rashad Khalifa and "code 19"

rows.thesis: Khalifa claimed to be a messenger on the basis of a numerical pattern ("code 19") in the Quran, and removed two verses that did not fit. A pattern in an already-miraculous text is not a new miracle, and a theory that requires deleting verses is falsified by the text.
rows.arg:
P1 A claim to be a messenger needs a miracle that proves it, and a theory about the Quran must fit the Quran. 
 P2 Numerical patterns in the Quran would be part of the Quran's own miracle, not a credential for Khalifa; and his code required removing 9:128-129, which are in the earliest manuscripts. 
 ∴ Khalifa's claim fails.
rows.ev:
The Quran was already a miracle; finding patterns in it adds nothing to Khalifa's personal claim.

 To make his counts work, Khalifa declared 9:128-129 not part of the Quran, though they are in first-century manuscripts (see Aisha's age & Surah at-Tawbah ).

 The Quran says Muhammad ﷺ is "the seal of the prophets" (33:40), and Khalifa's reinterpretation of that to allow a later "messenger" contradicts the consensus of the entire community.

Your opponent says
 “Code 19 is a mathematical miracle that proves Rashad was a messenger.”
 Answer it in your head first, then compare.
 Show a model answer Any long text contains patterns if you choose what to count, and Khalifa deleted two verses that broke his count. A pattern in the Quran would be the Quran's miracle, not his.

title: No prophet after Muhammad ﷺ (against Ahmadis)

rows.thesis: The Quran calls Muhammad ﷺ the seal of the prophets and declares the religion perfected. Mirza Ghulam Ahmad's claims rely on a forged gospel and on misreading the Quran about Jesus' death.

title: The Companions are praised by the Quran (against Shia polemics)
